questions.question_text: Of the following parasomnias, which one is more common in females than males?
questions.explanation:
No gender difference has been reported in sleepwalking, sleep terrors, or confusional arousals. Nightmares are reported to be more common in females. REM sleep behaviour disorder is more common in males, particularly those over the age of 50 years.
Ref: Singh S et al. Parasomnias: a comprehensive review. Cureus. 2018 Dec 10(12).
The correct answer is: Nightmares

questions.question_text: On corneal examination, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often present in patients with
questions.explanation:
Wilson disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various organs, primarily the liver and brain. The clinical symptoms are a result of organ dysfunction due to the direct or indirect e!ects of copper accumulation. Wilson disease is typically described as a hepatoneurological disease, with focus on signs of liver disease and extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g. wing-beating tremor and dystonia). Copper accumulates in multiple organs over the course of the disease, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations, including neurologic (40-50% at diagnosis), psychiatric (10-25% at diagnosis, and up to 100% over the disease course), ophthalmologic (KayserFleischer rings and sunflower cataracts) and occasionally endocrinologic, cardiologic, or/or osteoskeletal. Kayser-Fleischer rings are green-blue corneal deposits.Ref: Litwin T et al. Psychiatric manifestations in Wilson’s disease: possibilities and difficulties for treatment. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2018 Jul;8(7):199-211.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.
The correct answer is: Wilson disease

questions.question_text: Which of the following is preserved in associative visual agnosia?
questions.explanation:
Neurologic conditions such as strokes and other focal lesions have facilitated the definition of several disorders of visual perception. Apperceptive visual agnosia is the inability to identify and draw items using visual cues, with preservation of other sensory modalities. It represents failure of transmission of information from the higher visual sensory pathway to the association areas and is caused by bilateral lesions in the visual association areas. Associative visual agnosia is the inability to name or use objects despite the ability to draw them. It is caused by bilateral medial occipitotemporal lesions and can occur along with other visual impairments.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 927.
The correct answer is: Drawing objects

questions.question_text: Which of the following tremors is amplified as a target is reached?
questions.explanation:
Ref: Crawford III PF, Zimmerman EE. Tremor: Sorting through the differential diagnosis. American family physician. 2018 Feb 1;97(3):180-6.
The correct answer is: Cerebellar tremor

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency unit by his wife. He had breakfast that morning, but appeared unable to remember that he and his wife had planned a day out. He repeatedly enquired where she was taking him. She reports that he appeared bewildered, but was alert and had no sensory and motor deficits throughout. He returned to a normal mental state after 10 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The fundamental clinical feature of transient global amnesia (TGA) is the acute onset of amnesia. During an attack, patients cannot memorise or learn new information, that is, they have anterograde amnesia. They also cannot recall information acquired very recently, such as the events in the last several hours or days (i.e., they also have retrograde amnesia). Most patients seem calm but bewildered. TGA lasts for 3 to 24 hours but is most severe during the initial 1-2 hours. By definition, the total duration must not exceed 24 hours.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 113.
The correct answer is: Transient global amnesia
th

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in angle closure glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Angle closure is the form of glaucoma that can be induced or worsened by psychotropic medication. Topiramate has been associated with the development of closed-angle glaucoma, potentially due to swelling of the lens and ciliary body.
Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 520.
The correct answer is: Topiramate

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the best available evidence for the treatment of depression following a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Antidepressants are best avoided in the first 2 months following a myocardial infarction. If clinically indicated, SSRIs (sertraline is the drug of choice; avoid fluvoxamine and citalopram/escitalopram) should be prescribed rather than TCAs. If sedation is required, consider use of mirtazapine or a small dose of trazodone at night.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 1033.
The correct answer is: Sertraline

questions.question_text: What is the risk of depression in a cardiac patient with congestive heart failure compared to the general population?
questions.explanation:
Clinically significant depressive symptoms affect 21.5% of heart failure (HF) patients, with one-third of HF patients reporting elevated depressive symptoms on questionnaires and 19% meeting criteria for a depressive disorder (typically major depressive disorder, but some studies have included dysthymia and minor depression). These prevalence rates are similar in studies of inpatients and outpatients, and they are approximately two-to-three times higher than the general population.
Ref: Celano CM et al. Depression and anxiety in heart failure: a review. Harvard review of psychiatry. 2018 Jul;26(4):175.
The correct answer is: 3:1

questions.question_text: The mean age of onset of chronic fatigue syndrome is between
questions.explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) predominantly affects adults, with a peak age of onset between 20 and 45 years, and a fernale to male ratio of 3:1. The average age of onset is 33 years, but CFS can develop in people as old as 77 years. Patients can be ill for years or even decades. They most commonly report a fluctuating illness pattern in which symptoms wax and wane but are always present.
Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.
Bateman L et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: essentials of diagnosis and management. In Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2021 Nov 1 (Vol. 96, No. 11, pp. 2861-2878).
The correct answer is: 29-35 years

questions.question_text: The ratio of prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome in males compared to females is
questions.explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) predominantly a!ects adults, with a peak age of onset between 20 and 45 years, and a male to female ratio of 1:3. The average age of onset is 33 years, but CFS can develop in people as old as 77 years. Patients can be ill for years or even decades. They most commonly report a fluctuating illness pattern in which symptoms wax and wane but are always present.
Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.
Bateman L et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: essentials of diagnosis and management. In Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2021 Nov 1 (Vol. 96, No. 11, pp. 2861-2878).
The correct answer is: 1:3

questions.question_text: Diagnostic features of chronic fatigue syndrome include all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a debilitating disease with core symptoms of fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction. The aetiology of the illness has yet to be revealed, which has led to no established objective diagnostics, pathophysiology, or therapeutics. Accordingly, many expert groups have developed case definitions based on clinical features. To date, over 20 ME/CFS case definitions have been established by di!erent groups in various countries. The most widely used have been the Fukuda criteria and the international criteria.
A case of ME/CFS is defined by the presence of an unexplained, persistent, and relapsing chronic fatigue of new onset that is not alleviated by rest, which results in a significant reduction in the quality of life, and a concurrent occurrence of four or more of the following eight symptoms that must have persisted during six or more consecutive months:
1)      ‘Brain fog’ – described as impairment in short-term memory or concentration severe enough to cause a reduction in previous levels of personal activities
2)      Sore throat
3)      Tender cervical or axillary nodes
4)      Muscle pain
5)      Multipoint pain without joint swelling
6)      Headaches
7)      Unrefreshing sleep
8)      Post-exertional malaise lasting more than 24 hours
Ref: Lim EJ, Son CG. Review of case definitions for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Journal of translational medicine. 2020 Dec;18(1):1-10.
Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.
The correct answer is: Duration >12 months

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman has a history of 2 episodes of unilateral blindness that lasted for few weeks. She now presents with paraesthesia of the left leg. An MRI shows multiple demyelinating plaques. Which of the following is correct with respect to her illness?

options.text: It has a uniform, progressive course
It is due to a bacterial infection
It presents with diverse physical signs
It is more common in men than women
It occurs more commonly near the equator

correct_answer.text: It presents with diverse physical signs

correct_answers.text: It presents with diverse physical signs

questions.explanation:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease. The cause is uncertain, but likely due to environmental factors (e.g. Epstein-Barr virus infection, vitamin D deficiency, latitude, and smoking) interacting with genetic predisposition. MS is twice as common in women as in men. It is seen with greater frequency as the distance from the equator increases (i.e. in White populations living in northern latitudes). It is characterized by multiple demyelinating lesions with a predilection for the optic nerves, cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord. MS is predominantly a white matter disease. Diverse physical signs reflect the presence and distribution of plaques. 85-90% of cases start with episode of acute neurological symptoms (e.g. optic neuritis). Most patients follow a relapsing-remitting course.
Ref: Ron MA. The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. BJPsych Advances. 2018 May,24(3):178-87.
The correct answer is: It presents with diverse physical signs

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not characteristic of chronic fatigue syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome is a disabling clinical condition characterised by unexplained and persistent post-exertional fatigue accompanied by a variety of symptoms related to cognitive, immunological, endocrinological, and autonomic dysfunction. It is also characterised by a substantial reduction in previous levels of occupational, educational, social, and personal activities. Unemployment rates among those who su!er from CFS are between 35-69%.
Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.
The correct answer is: Significant weight loss

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of sleep terrors?

options.text: Vivid memory of dreams on waking up

questions.explanation:
Sleep terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterised by a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic arousal. The individual usually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive to stimuli (e.g conversation) during the episode. Sleep terrors typically occur during the first third of the night, during slow-wave stage 3 of NREM sleep. Autonomic hyperactivity is manifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils, agitation, tremulousness, and increased muscle tone. Episodes usually last for 5-10 minutes.
Ref: Leung AK et al. Sleep terrors: an updated review. Current pediatric reviews. 2020 Aug 1;16(3):176-82.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 462.
The correct answer is: Increased muscle tone

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of subcortical dementia?
questions.explanation:
Cortical dementias consist of illnesses in which neuropsychologic signs of cortical dysfunction – typically aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia – accompany dementia. Because the brain’s subcortical areas are relatively untouched, patients remain alert, attentive, and ambulatory. Alzheimer disease serves as the prime example of a cortical dementia. In contrast, subcortical dementias are typified by a!ective change, and slowed mental processing, which overshadow cognitive impairment. Gait abnormalities constitute the other core feature. Prime examples are Parkinson disease, NPH, HIV-associated dementia, vascular cognitive impairment, and MS.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 115.
Shaik SS, Varma AR. Di!erentiating the dementias: a neurological approach. Progress in Neurology and Psychiatry. 2012 Jan;16(1):11-8.
The correct answer is: Parkinson disease dementia
th

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old woman has been referred by her dentist for a long history of facial tingling, numbness, nausea and temporomandibular joint pain. Her symptoms have been anatomically inconsistent, and the pain has tended to fluctuate. She has insisted on multiple investigations, which have shown no abnormalities. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by the presence of bodily symptoms that are distressing to the individual and excessive attention toward the symptoms, which may be manifest by repeated contact with health care providers. Bodily symptoms are persistent, being present on most days for at least several months. Typically, bodily distress disorder involves multiple bodily symptoms that may vary over time. Occasionally there is a single symptom – usually pain or fatigue – that is associated with the other features of the disorder. The symptoms and associated distress and preoccupation have at least some impact on the individual’s functioning.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 867.
International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
The correct answer is: Bodily distress disorder

questions.question_text: A cognitive faculty commonly affected in patients with post-concussion syndrome is
questions.explanation:
Attention deficits and impairment of processing speed are commonly seen in mild traumatic brain injury and post-concussion syndrome. Situational factors contributing to neuropsychological disability in these cases include rapid processing demands, need for complex cognitive attention, and external distractions.
Ref: Broshek DK et al. A review of post-concussion syndrome and psychological factors associated with concussion. Brain injury. 2015 Jan 28;29(2):228-37.
Kaltiainen H et al. Mild traumatic brain injury affects cognitive processing and modifies oscillatory brain activity during attentional tasks. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2019 Jul 15:36(14):2222-32.
The correct answer is: Speed of processing

questions.question_text: Which of the following are commonly seen in patients with post-concussion syndrome?

options.text: Short term memory loss and personality changes
Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

correct_answer.text: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

correct_answers.text: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

questions.explanation:
Post-concussion syndrome is characterised by one or more core symptoms – headache, memory impairment, and insomnia – lasting more than 2 to 3 months after a head injury. These and other symptoms of post-concussion syndrome – including irritability, sleepiness, tinnitus – remain entirely subjective and often nonspecific, variable, and occasionally unending. Patients with post-concussion syndrome characteristically describe mild amnesia accompanied by inattention or easy distractibility, slowed information processing, and difficulty completing complex mental tasks. Post-concussion syndrome patients also often report dizziness. In most cases, the dizziness is not authentic vertigo, but a nonspecific sensation with variable, idiosyncratic meanings that substitutes for lightheadedness, anxiety, unsteadiness, or lassitude. Patients have a normal physical and neurologic examination, CT, and MRI. Although the EEG may show minor abnormalities, the changes are generally inconsistent, insignificant, and often attributable to medications.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 559-560.
The correct answer is: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing
th

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old woman is 6 months pregnant. She is depressed, has a previous history of depression, and a family history of depression. She has responded well to paroxetine in the past. If she were to take paroxetine for the remainder of her pregnancy, which of the following e!ects is most likely to be seen in the newborn?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs do not appear to be major teratogens, with most data supporting the safety of fluoxetine. When taken late in pregnancy, SSRIs may increase the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; the absolute risk is very low. Women who take SSRIs may be at increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage. The neonate may experience discontinuation symptoms, which are usually mild (such as agitation or irritability), or rarely respiratory distress and convulsions, with SSRIs. The risk is particularly high with short half-life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 685-689.
The correct answer is: Irritability

questions.question_text: As a member of the hospital consultation-liaison team, you decide to prescribe an antidepressant for a 65-year-old man who has recently su!ered a stroke whilst on warfarin. You are concerned about antidepressants interacting with warfarin, but want to prescribe the antidepressant that is best supported by the current evidence base. What will be your choice of medication?
questions.explanation:
According to the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines, SSRIs continue to be the most preferred, evidence-based class of drugs for post-stroke depression. If the index stroke was haemorrhagic, we need to be cautious about SSRIs increasing the risk of further haemorrhages, especially if the patient had to continue anticoagulation for other reasons. If the patient is taking warfarin or other oral anticoagulants, the guidelines suggest using citalopram or escitalopram as they probably have the lowest interaction potential with warfarin among all SSRIs and use the lowest e!ective dose.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 362.
Mortensen JK, Andersen G. Pharmacological management of post-stroke depression: an update of the evidence and clinical guidance. Expert Opinion on Pharmacotherapy. 2021 Jun 13;22(9):1157-66.
The correct answer is: Escitalopram

questions.question_text: Which of the following pregnant mothers has the highest risk of having a child with ADHD?

options.text: 30 year old woman who drinks one glass of red wine a day
31 year old woman who drinks 3 mugs of coffee a day
21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day
26 year old woman who has no substance use habits
22 year old woman who smokes one joint of marijuana a day

correct_answer.text: 21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day

correct_answers.text: 21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day

questions.explanation:
Maternal smoking during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of ADHD in children. Maternal pre-pregnancy obesity and overweight, pre-eclampsia, hypertension, acetaminophen exposure, and smoking during pregnancy are strongly associated with ADHD.
Ref: He Y et al. Maternal smoking during pregnancy and ADHD: results from a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies. Journal of attention disorders. 2020 Oct 24(12):1637-47.
Kim JH et al. Environmental risk factors, protective factors, and peripheral biomarkers for ADHD: an umbrella review. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2020 Nov 1;7(11):955-70.
The correct answer is: 21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day

questions.question_text: A 21-year-old woman has been diagnosed with postpartum depression and is currently receiving antidepressant treatment. Which observer rating would be most appropriate to use to assess her response to treatment?
questions.explanation:
The Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRaS) is a 10-item observer-rated scale. Each item is rated 0-6, with a total score obtained. Response to an antidepressant is usually defined as a 50% or more decrease from baseline on the MADRaS, and remission is defined as a score of 10 or less. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item tool developed for screening screening postpartum women for depression in outpatient clinics, home visits, or during postpartum appointments.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 97.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 603.
Smith-Nielsen J et al. Validation of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale against both DSM-5 and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for depression. BMC psychiatry. 2018 Dec;18(1):1-2.
The correct answer is: Montgomery Asberg depression rating scale

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to the mechanism of action of modafinil?

options.text: It inhibits noradrenaline in the hypothalamus
It reduces dopamine in the nucleus accumbens
It activates neurons that release orexin

correct_answer.text: It activates neurons that release orexin

correct_answers.text: It activates neurons that release orexin

questions.explanation:
Exactly how modafinil works is unknown, but it is clearly different from classical stimulants such as methylphenidate and amphetamine. Blockade of the dopamine transporter (DAT) by modafinil leads to increased tonic dopaminergic firing and downstream effects on wake-promoting neurotransmitters. Specifically, cortical release of wake-promoting neurotransmitters is increased, which leads to downstream release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus and further activation of the lateral hypothalamus, with corresponding orexin release that stabilises wakefulness. Modafinil activates hypothalamic neurons that release orexin/hypocretin. The elimination half-life of modafinil is 10-12 hours.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 521-523.
Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 445.
The correct answer is: It activates neurons that release orexin

questions.question_text: Modafinil, which is used for daytime sleepiness, causes which of the following neurochemical changes?
questions.explanation:
Increased synaptic dopamine following blockade of the dopamine transmitter by modafinil leads to increased tonic firing and downstream effects on neurotransmitters involved in wakefulness. Specifically, this leads to downstream release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus and further activation of the lateral hypothalamus, with corresponding orexin release that stabilises wakefulness. Modafinil activates hypothalamic neurons that release orexin/hypocretin. The elimination half-life of modafinil is 10-12 hours.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 444-445.
Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 521-523.
The correct answer is: Increased synaptic dopamine

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common side effect of modafinil?
questions.explanation:
Modafinil most commonly causes headache (dose-dependent). Other notable side effects include anxiety, nervousness, insomnia, dry mouth, diarrhoea, nausea, anorexia, pharyngitis, rhinitis, hypertension, and palpitations. Modafinil can cause CNS effects similar to those caused by other CNS agents (e.g. changes in mood and, theoretically, activation of psychosis, mania, or suicidal ideation).
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 522-523.
The correct answer is: Headache

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants has an e!ect in common with antinausea drugs such as ondansetron?
questions.explanation:
Mirtazapine has 5HT3 antagonism action. The 5HT3 receptors best known to clinicians are perhaps those localised in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the brainstem - where they mediate nausea and vomiting, especially in response to cancer chemotherapy - and also those localised in the gastrointestinal tract itself - where they mediate nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea/bowel motility when stimulated by serotonin. Blocking these 5HT3 receptors can therefore protect against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as well as against serotonin-induced gastrointestinal side e!ects that can accompany agents that increase serotonin. Oral disintegrating tablets of mirtazapine have been used peri-operatively for nausea.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 Edition. 2021. pp. 309-311.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 891.
The correct answer is: Mirtazapine
th

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic sign of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation:
Patients with hepatic encephalopathy have asterixis. Asterixis can be elicited by having patients extend their arms and hands as though they were stopping traffic. Their hands intermittently quickly fall forward and slowly return, as though flapping or waving good-bye.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. pp. 136-137.
The correct answer is: Asterixis

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman is brought for urgent assessment by her husband. He reports that she seems to be hearing voices and 'seeing things', and that her mood has been unstable. She has no insight into these mental status changes but is concerned about a rash on her face. Her husband also reports that she might have had a seizure the other day, but she refused to come for assessment. Of the following, what is her most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The multisystem autoimmune disorder systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is most common in women in their 30s. Neuropsychiatric symptoms are common. Seizures, cranial nerve palsies, peripheral neuropathy, 'spinal stroke', and other focal signs may occur, in addition to the common dermatological, rheumatological, haematological, and cardiovascular manifestation of the disorder. Depression and anxiety disorders are very common in patients with SLE. Psychosis is a rare manifestation, the most common being secondary to glucocorticoid treatment. Psychosis usually precedes or occurs early in the evolution of the disease, is associated with lupus activity, and usually has a good prognosis after treatment.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 150-151.
Carrión-Barberà I et al. Neuropsychiatric involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus: a review. Autoimmunity Reviews. 2021 Apr 1:20(4):102780.
The correct answer is: Systemic lupus erythematosus

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old man with a history of stroke now presents with right-sided drooping of the mouth and flattening of the right nasolabial fold. He is able to furrow his forehead and close both of his eyes. What is the likely cause of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
The facial nerves supply the ‘muscles of facial expression’. Each facial nerve supplies its ipsilateral temporalis, orbicularis oculi, and orbicularis oris muscles – muscles responsible for a frown, raised eyebrows, wink, smile, and grimace. In a unique and potentially confusing arrangement in their neuroanatomy, each cerebral hemisphere innervates both the contralateral and ipsilateral facial nerve motor nuclei. In the classical explanation, because of their crossed and uncrossed supply, both cerebral hemispheres innervate the upper facial muscles, but only the contralateral cerebral hemisphere innervates the lower facial muscles. Facial nerve injuries cause ipsilateral paresis of both upper and lower face muscles. This pattern is termed a ‘peripheral facial’ or ‘lower motor neuron’ weakness. In contrast, injuries of the cerebral cortex or upper brainstem, which interrupt the corticobulbar tract, cause paresis of only the lower contralateral face. This pattern is termed a ‘central’ or ‘upper motor neuron’ weakness.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 33-35.
The correct answer is: Facial nerve palsy (upper motor neuron)
th

questions.question_text: In which of the following neurological conditions is anaemia a common finding?
questions.explanation:
Subacute combined degeneration is a demyelinated disease commonly associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. It is commonly accompanied by anaemia.
Ref: Cao J, Su ZY, Xu SB, Liu CC. Subacute combined degeneration: a retrospective study of 68 cases with short-term follow-up. European Neurology. 2018;79(5-6):247-55.
The correct answer is: Subacute combined degeneration

questions.question_text: The prevalence of co-morbid depression in those with coronary heart disease is approximately
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of depression is significantly higher in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD). More than 20% of patients with CHD are depressed, with the risk of depression highest in those with more severe CHD. CHD patients with depression are at increased risk for recurrent cardiovascular events and mortality.
Ref: De Hert M et al. The intriguing relationship between coronary heart disease and mental disorders. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2018 Mar;20(1):31.
The correct answer is: 20%

questions.question_text: Compared to the general population, suicide rates in patients with Huntington disease are
questions.explanation:
Suicidal ideation/attempts are common in Huntington disease. Rates of suicide are approximately 4 times higher than the general population. Risk of suicide is correlated with family history of suicide, history of previous attempts, and presence of depression, especially in prodromal stages.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.
Kachian ZR et al. Suicidal ideation and behavior in Huntington's disease: Systematic review and recommendations. Journal of a!ective disorders. 2019 May 1;250:319-29.
The correct answer is: 4 times higher

questions.question_text: Amnesia is commonly seen in the setting of
questions.explanation:
Herpes simplex encephalitis causes amnesia accompanied by personality changes, focal impaired awareness seizures (previously named complex partial seizures), and the Kluver-Bucy syndrome because the virus typically enters the undersurface of the brain through the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporal lobes. This condition occurs relatively frequently because herpes simplex is the most common cause of sporadically occurring (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis. In contrast, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) encephalitis does not cause this picture.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 112.
The correct answer is: Herpes simplex encephalitis
th

questions.question_text: Which of the following occurs in Ganser syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 236.
Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1-22.
The correct answer is: Pseudohallucinations

questions.question_text: A patient with bipolar disorder and a history of mixed affective states is in the first trimester of her pregnancy. She has not been on any medications of late, but is very concerned about the possibility of relapse. Of the following, what would be the preferred medication to prescribe to her?
questions.explanation:
For pregnant women with bipolar disorder who have had a long period without relapse, the possibility of switching to a safer drug (antipsychotic) or withdrawing treatment completely before conception and for at least the first trimester should be considered. No mood stabiliser is clearly safe. NICE recommends the use of mood stabilising antipsychotics as a preferable alternative to a mood stabiliser.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 692.
The correct answer is: Olanzapine

questions.question_text: Which one of the following medications could be used to treat pathologic crying?
questions.explanation:
The most conspicuous feature of pseudobulbar palsy is emotional lability. With little or no provocation, patients tend to burst into tears or, less often, laughter, with no apparent change in their mood. These unprovoked emotional expressions are referred to as pathologic laughing and crying, pseudobulbar affect, or involuntary emotional expression disorder. Amitriptyline, SSRIs (such as citalopram), or a combination of dextromethorphan and quinidine may suppress this.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 39.
The correct answer is: Citalopram

questions.question_text: A pregnant bipolar patient has no other treatment option but to continue valproate. Which of the following should she take in addition?
questions.explanation:
Valproate is an established human teratogen. Usually, valproate should be reserved for post-menopausal women only. Its use in younger women should be treatment of last resort. There is no evidence that folate protects against anticonvulsant-induced neural tube defects if given during pregnancy, but may do so if given prior to conception (the neural tube is essentially formed by 8 weeks of pregnancy before many women realise they are pregnant). However, folate supplementation may be beneficial for early neurodevelopment and so should always be offered.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 260, 680, 691.
The correct answer is: Folate

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most appropriate medication to prescribe for a pregnant woman with first-episode depression?
questions.explanation: initiating an antidepressant during pregnancy, previous response to treatment must be taken into account (i.e. consider using previously effective treatment). For previously untreated patients, consider sertraline (least placental exposure). When taken in late pregnancy, SSRIs may increase risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension the newborn, though the absolute risk is very low. The risk with sertraline may be lower than with other SSRIs. Neonates may experience discontinuation symptoms, usually mild, with SSRIs. The risk is particularly high with short half-life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following favours psychogenic nonepileptic seizures rather than epileptic seizures?
questions.explanation: Ictal eye closure has been assessed in several controlled studies and is significantly more frequent in psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) than epileptic seizures (ES). Closed eyes during an attack is considered a discriminator between PNES and ES. The mean duration of PNES is longer than ES. There is considerable evidence to suggest that a duration of more than 2 minutes is highly suggestive of PNES, although this is an arbitrary limit. Duration of longer than 10 minutes strongly suggests PNES. In studies that have compared convulsive PNES with generalised tonic clonic seizures, the proportion of events with side-to-side head or body movement, especially with coordinated agonist and antagonist activity, are significantly higher in PNES.

questions.question_text: Idiopathic progressive calcium deposition in the basal ganglia is seen in
questions.explanation:
Fahr disease, also known as idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by bilateral calcifications in multiple basal ganglia. Patients with Fahr disease may be asymptomatic or present with movement disorders such as parkinsonism, psychiatric disorders such as psychosis and depression, cognitive impairment, dementia, and a variety of other symptoms. The age on onset is mostly between 40 and 50 years, but the symptoms can manifest at any age. Patients who become symptomatic early in adulthood mostly develop psychiatric or cognitive disorders, like psychosis, whereas patients who become symptomatic later in life develop mainly movement disorders in combination with other clinical features.
Ref: Peters ME et al. Mechanisms of calcification in Fahr disease and exposure of potential therapeutic targets. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 Oct 1;10(5):449-57.
The correct answer is: Fahr disease

questions.question_text: Presence of which of the following should prompt investigations for a medical cause of recurrent anxiety?

options.text: Onset of symptoms before the age of 25 years

questions.explanation:
Once e!ective treatment has been adequately delivered and adhered to, there will be a proportion of patients with anxiety that have not remitted and a smaller proportion that remain quite symptomatic. At this point, it should be considered whether there are exogenous factors that are aggravating and/or maintaining anxiety, whether there is a medical condition, and whether the diagnosis may be wrong or incomplete (i.e. whether there is a comorbidity present that is accounting for the poor response to treatment).
Ref: Roy-Byrne P. Treatment-refractory anxiety; definition, risk factors, and treatment challenges. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2015 Jun;17(2):191.
The correct answer is: Poor response to anxiolytic agents

questions.question_text: Which of the following is more indicative of HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy rather than HIV-associated dementia?
questions.explanation:
Because HIV-associated dementia (HAD) develops rapidly – over several weeks to a few months – it is considered a rapidly progressive dementia. Psychomotor retardation, loss of dexterity, and gait impairment are so characteristic that HAD is considered a prime example of subcortical dementia. HAD patients initially remain verbal and articulate. Later, reticence, apathy, and withdrawal predominate. Even in the elderly, the rapidity of onset and presence of psychomotor retardation and gait impairment readily separate the clinical picture of HAD from Alzheimer disease. Vacuolar myelopathy is associated with advanced HIV infection. Patients present with ataxic gait, slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, dorsal column-type sensory loss, incontinence, and erectile dysfunction. If HIV testing has not yet been done, it is important to consider HIV testing in patients with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis and/or progressive cognitive impairment.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 134.
Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 375.
Asaduzzaman M et al. HIV-Associated Vacuolar Myelopathy and HIV-Associated Neurocognitive Disorder as an Initial Presentation in HIV Infection. Case Reports in Infectious Diseases. 2023 Jan; 1-7.
The correct answer is: Spastic paraparesis

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric symptom in Cushing syndrome is
questions.explanation:
Cushing syndrome is a relatively rare but serious condition that results from chronic hypercortisolism. Depression is the most prevalent and significant psychiatric disorder among patients with Cushing syndrome.
Ref: Lin TY et al. Psychiatric symptoms in Cushing’s syndrome: a systematic review. Innovations in Clinical Neuroscience. 2020 Jan 1;17(1-3):30.
The correct answer is: Depression

questions.question_text: Which of the following MRI findings is characteristically seen in Huntington disease?
questions.explanation:
Huntington disease is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system, with a genetic autosomal dominant inheritance, that first involves the basal ganglia (caudate nucleus and putamen) and results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene. In Huntington disease, CT/MRI show atrophy of the basal ganglia (caudate and putamen) with ‘boxing’ of the caudate and dilatation of the ventricles.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.
The correct answer is: Caudate atrophy

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a history of depression and is about to receive treatment for multiple sclerosis. Which of the following medications should prompt prophylactic treatment with an antidepressant?
questions.explanation:
The role of interferon-beta in the aetiology of multiple sclerosis (MS) depression is unclear, but it is now thought that depression occurs no more frequently in people treated with interferon-beta. Standard care for initiation of interferonbeta should include assessment for depression and, for those with a past history of depressive illness, prophylactic treatment with an antidepressant.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 808.
The correct answer is: Interferon-beta

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with diabetes is brought to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and muscle cramps. He has been diagnosed with depression and recently started on fluoxetine. What is the most likely metabolic complication?
questions.explanation:
Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. The most likely mechanism of this adverse e!ect is the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). There is a strong level of supporting evidence that SSRIs (including fluoxetine) are associated with a relatively high risk of hyponatraemia. All patients taking antidepressants should be informed of and observed for signs of hyponatraemia (dizziness, nausea, lethargy, confusion, cramps, seizures).
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 393-394.
The correct answer is: Hyponatraemia

questions.question_text: Of the following, which is most recommended for the treatment for post-stroke depression based on the best available evidence?
questions.explanation:
Treatment of post-stroke depression is complicated by medical co-morbidities and by the potential for interactions with other co-prescribed drugs (especially warfarin). Contraindications to antidepressant treatment are more likely with tricyclics than with SSRIs. Fluoxetine, citalopram, and nortriptyline are probably the most studied and seem to be effective and safe. SSRIs and nortriptyline are widely recommended for post-stroke depression. Reboxetine (which, like nortriptyline, does not affect platelet activity) may also be effective and well tolerated, although its effects overall are doubtful. Vortioxetine may be of particular interest owing to its additional benefits on cognition (independent of effects on depressive symptoms). It also does not appear to adversely affect cardiovascular parameters or interact with warfarin or aspirin, but there are currently no data to support its use specifically in post-stroke depression.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 362.
The correct answer is: sertraline

questions.question_text: Which of the following is appropriate to screen women for postpartum depression?
questions.explanation:
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item tool developed for screening postpartum women for depression in outpatient clinics, home visits, or during postpartum appointments.
Ref: Smith-Nielsen J et al. Validation of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale against both DSM-5 and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for depression. BMC psychiatry. 2018 Dec;18(1):1-2.
The correct answer is: Edinburgh Depression Scale

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, which of the following is included under dissociative disorders?
questions.explanation:
The ICD-11 divides ICD-10 possession trance disorder into the separate diagnoses of trance disorder and possession trance disorder. The separation reflects the distinctive features in possession trance disorder wherein the customary sense of personal identity is replaced by an external “possessing“ identity attributed to the influence of a spirit, power, deity, or other spiritual entity. In addition, a greater range of more complex behaviours may be exhibited in possession trance disorder, while trance disorder typically involves the repetition of a small repertoire of simpler behaviours.
Ref: Reed GM et al. Innovations and changes in the ICD-11 classification of mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. World Psychiatry. 2019 Feb;18(1):3-19.
The correct answer is: Possession trance disorder

questions.question_text: What is the untreated case fatality rate in patients with herpes simplex encephalitis?
questions.explanation:
Before the use of acyclovir, the (untreated) case fatality rate of herpes simplex encephalitis was up to 70%. Although acyclovir administered intravenously has substantially improved outcomes for HSV encephalitis (mortality reduced from 70% untreated to 8% treated), 35% of those who survive still have long-term neuropsychiatric disabilities including cognitive and seizure disorders.
Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.
Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-.
The correct answer is: 70%

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a condition classified in ICD-11’s new sexual health chapter?
questions.explanation:
ICD-10 gender identity disorders have been renamed as ‘gender incongruence’ in ICD-11 and moved from the mental disorders chapter to the new sexual health chapter, meaning that a transgender identity is no longer considered a mental disorder. ICD-11 guidelines explicitly state that gender variant behaviour and preference alone are not sufficient for making a diagnosis of gender incongruence. ICD-11 paraphilic disorders include exhibitionistic disorder, voyeuristic disorder, pedophilic disorder, coercive sexual sadism disorder, and frotteuristic disorder. ICD-10 categories of sadomasochism, fetishism, and fetishistic transvestism have been eliminated.
Ref: Reed GM et al. Innovations and changes in the ICD-11 classification of mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. World Psychiatry. 2019 Feb;18(1):3-19.
The correct answer is: Gender incongruence

questions.question_text: A 33 year old man has intractable seizures. Which of the following may support a diagnosis of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures rather than epileptic seizures?

options.text: Loss of body tone during a seizure

questions.explanation:
Ref: Xiang X et al. Di!erential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures based on semiology. Acta Epileptologica. 2019 Dec;1(1):1-5.
The correct answer is: Regaining alertness and orientation rapidly

questions.question_text: A 52-year-old patient in palliative care has both depression and co-morbid pain. Which of the following medications should be chosen for the treatment of her depression?
questions.explanation:
In the setting of palliative care, no clinically significant differences in terms of efficacy have been shown amongst the most commonly used antidepressants. Given equivalent efficacy, an antidepressant should be chosen based on considerations of: (1) activating versus sedating features, (2) tolerability, and (3) potentially useful side effects or other indications of the antidepressant. It is recommended to choose escitalopram or sertraline for tolerability, duloxetine if there is co-morbid pain, duloxetine or bupropion if there is a melancholic presentation of depression, and methylphenidate if the patient is at the end of life.
Ref: Riordan PA et al. Top ten tips palliative care clinicians should know about psychopharmacology. Journal of palliative medicine. 2019 May 1;22(5):572-9.
The correct answer is: Duloxetine

questions.question_text: MRI may show hypointensity of the striatum in patients with
questions.explanation:
Fahr disease, also known as idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by bilateral calcifications in multiple basal ganglia. Patients with Fahr disease may be asymptomatic or present with movement disorders such as parkinsonism, psychiatric disorders such as psychosis and depression, cognitive impairment, dementia, and a variety of other symptoms. This variability in symptoms can partly be explained by the division of the basal ganglia into dorsal and ventral systems. The dorsal striatum plays a major role in motor and cognitive functions, whereas the ventral striatum plays a role in motivational functions. Calcifications in Fahr disease are present as high-density areas on CT scans but can be more difficult to detect with conventional MRI sequences in early stages. Calcified lesions can appear hypointense in T2-weighted images, because of the presence of other minerals in the same areas and the di!erence in the composition of calcium deposits, such as zinc, manganese, iron, and magnesium.
Ref: Peters ME et al. Mechanisms of calcification in Fahr disease and exposure of potential therapeutic targets. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 Oct 1;10(5):449-57.
Donzuso G et al. Basal ganglia calcifications (Fahr’s syndrome): related conditions and clinical features. Neurological Sciences. 2019 Nov;40:2251-63.
The correct answer is: Fahr disease

questions.question_text: 'Baby blues' are experience by up to what proportion of new mothers?
questions.explanation:
Up to three-quarters of new mothers will experience a short-lived period of tearfulness and emotional lability, starting 2-3 days after birth and lasting 1-2 days, called ‘baby blues’. This is easily recognisable by midwifery sta! and requires only reassurance and observation towards resolution. There is weak evidence that it may relate to post-partum reductions in the levels of oestrogen, progesterone, and prolactin (which occur around 72 hours after birth).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 494.
The correct answer is: 3 in 4

questions.question_text: Frequent medical visits, splitting of the treatment team, and high risk of iatrogenic harm are most associated with which of the following psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by the presence of bodily symptoms that are distressing to the individual and excessive attention toward the symptoms, which may be manifest by repeated contact with health care providers. Frequent medical visits and extensive interactions with the health care system often occur. There is a high risk of iatrogenic harm and iatrogenic substance dependence. Hostility and frustration can be felt on both sides of the doctor-patient relationship with splitting between members of the treating team.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 864.
International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
The correct answer is: Bodily distress disorder

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about bodily distress disorder?

options.text: The most frequent symptoms are non-specific and atypical
It is associated with significant psychological distress and functional impairment
It usually presents before the age of 40
Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system
Patients usually have long, complex medical histories

correct_answer.text: Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system

correct_answers.text: Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system

questions.explanation:
In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by repeated presentations with medically unexplained symptoms, a!ecting multiple organ systems, first presenting before the age of 40 years. It is usually chronic in adults, and is associated with significant psychological distress, functional impairment, and risk of iatrogenic harm. Patients have long, complex medical histories, although at interview, they may minimise all but the most recent symptomatology. The most frequent symptoms are non-specific and atypical.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 864.
The correct answer is: Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients will die by completed suicide in the 24 months after an initial act of self-harm?
questions.explanation:
Roughly 1% of patients will die by completed suicide in the 24 months after an initial act of self-harm, with the risk highest in the weeks following the original act. This represents a mortality by suicide 50-100 times that of the general population.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 848.
The correct answer is: 1%

questions.question_text: Risk factors for completed suicide include all except
questions.explanation:
Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. Risk to self: identifying and managing risk of suicide and self-harm. BJPsych Advances. 2021 Mar;27(2):126-36.
The correct answer is: Female sex

questions.question_text: Of the following, episodic panic attacks are reported most often in patients with
questions.explanation:
Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumour of the adrenal gland that produces catecholamines. It often presents with a classic triad of headache, palpitations, and generalised sweating. Anxiety is the fourth most common symptom and may mimic panic attacks.
Ref: Alguire C et al. Unusual presentation of pheochromocytoma: thirteen years of anxiety requiring psychiatric treatment. Endocrinology, diabetes & metabolism case reports. 2018 Apr 6;2018(1).
The correct answer is: Pheochromocytoma

questions.question_text: Which of the following age groups are at increased risk of traumatic brain injury compared to the general population?
questions.explanation:
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common cause of death and lifelong disability (largely due to neuropsychiatric sequelae) in young adults. Common causes are road traffic accidents, falls, and assaults. Alcohol is often a contributory factor. Improved life expectancy has, however, led to an increase in TBI in the frail elderly in high-income countries, shifting the peak incidence from 20s to 40s.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 172.
The correct answer is: Adolescents/young adults and frail elderly

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbid psychiatric condition associated with hypochondriasis is
questions.explanation:
Hypochondriasis has a particularly high co-morbidity with generalised anxiety disorder, over 50%. Hypochondriasis may also co-exist with major depressive illness, OCD, and panic disorder. Examination of the time course of symptom development and most prominent clinical features helps to distinguish primary hypochondriasis from a secondary clinical feature of these disorders.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 870.
The correct answer is: Generalized anxiety disorder

questions.question_text: Which lobe of the brain is most commonly affected in patients with herpes simplex encephalitis?
questions.explanation:
Herpes simplex encephalitis causes amnesia accompanied by personality changes, focal impaired awareness seizures (previously named complex partial seizures), and the Kluver-Bucy syndrome because the virus typically enters the undersurface of the brain through the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporal lobes. This condition occurs relatively frequently because herpes simplex is the most common cause of sporadically occurring (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 112.
The correct answer is: Temporal

questions.question_text: Mrs. P suffers from epilepsy and co-morbid depression. She has been tried on SSRIs with no benefit and is keen to try an older antidepressant. The safest choice in her case would be
questions.explanation:
Moclobemide is not known to be proconvulsive. Most TCAs are epileptogenic at higher doses (particularly clomipramine and amitriptyline). Bupropion has a dose-related risk of seizures.
Antidepressants in epilepsy:
=
Low risk: SSRIs, mirtazapine, duloxetine
Probably low risk: agomelatine, MAOIs, moclobemide, reboxetine, vortioxetine
Moderate risk: lithium, trazodone, venlafaxine, vilazodone
High risk: amoxapine, bupropion, maprotiline, TCAS
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 789.
The correct answer is: Moclobemide

questions.question_text: Which of the following is untrue with respect to investigations in herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE)?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging of choice in HSE
Gold standard for in vivo diagnosis is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes simplex virus
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination commonly reveals a lymphocytosis and raised protein
The EEG is invariably abnormal in HSE
CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

correct_answer.text: CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

correct_answers.text: CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

questions.explanation:
Brain abnormalities in herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) may be visible on CT but are much more consistently seen on MRI with gadolinium. MRI is the most sensitive method of detecting early lesions and is the imaging of choice in HSE. Brain MRI typically shows hyperintensities involving the cortex and white matter in T2 and FLAIR images - areas of contrast enhancement can also be present. Gold standard for HSE diagnosis is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for HSV which has a sensitivity and specificity of >95%. False negatives can occur in the first 72 hours of onset. Other supportive findings include CSF pleocytosis (increased lymphocytes) and raised protein, abnormalities on EEG, and brain lesions or enhancement involving the temporal lobe, orbitofrontal and/or insular cortex on MRI. The EEG in HSE is invariably abnormal. Non-specific slowing may be the only feature early in the illness; later stages are more likely to be associated with high voltage periodic lateralizing epileptiform discharges. If present, they are diagnostically useful, but are not specific for HSE.
Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.
Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-
The correct answer is: CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

questions.question_text: Most cases of herpes simplex encephalitis are caused by
questions.explanation:
Most cases of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) in adults are caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and occur equally in both sexes. Age >50 years is an important risk factor. HSE most frequently affects the medial temporal lobes, but can also affect the insular, cingulate, and frontobasal cortex.
Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.
Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-.
The correct answer is: Herpes simplex type 1
